overview.title: 📖 Overview: Counting and Recounting the Thirty-Six
overview.subtitle: Keritot 3a–3b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא שְׁנֵי לָאוִין וְכָרֵת אֶחָד – חַלֵּק חַטָּאת בֵּינֵיהֶן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues probing the mishna's list of thirty-six karet violations from every angle. It first denies that punishment can ever be derived by a fortiori logic alone, then lays down Rabbi Elazar's rule that wherever two distinct prohibitions share a single karet verse, one who transgresses both unwittingly must bring two separate sin offerings, illustrated by the anointing oil. The Gemara then asks a very practical question: since the list mixes prohibitions that only a man could violate with one only a woman could violate, who could ever transgress all thirty-six in one lapse? This sends the Gemara through several proposed edits to the list, and finally to Rav's own accounting of the number: thirty-three genuine unwitting-sin-offering cases, plus three added only to round out the karet count. The daf closes with a dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish over why the mishna's list includes the necromancer but omits the sorcerer, turning on whether a sin offering requires a physical action.

slides.title: 🚫 No Punishment by Inference
slides.subtitle: Can karet for a full sister be deduced from the karet stated for a half sister?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The Torah states karet separately for intercourse with a father's-side half sister and a mother's-side half sister. Why not simply infer, a fortiori, that a full sister — both father's and mother's daughter — is equally liable?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: One does not administer punishment based on an a fortiori inference (עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין). Even an airtight logical inference cannot generate a new punishment; the Torah must state it explicitly.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But Rabbi Yitzḥak disagrees — he holds one does administer punishment by a fortiori inference!

lines.speaker: Alt. answer
lines.text: Or, if you prefer: Rabbi Yitzḥak instead derives the karet for a full sister from the parallel prohibition (warning) stated for her — since she is explicitly forbidden, the same karet that applies to other forbidden relatives applies to her too.

callout.label: Underlying principle:
callout.text: Halakhic punishments, unlike prohibitions, cannot rest on logical inference alone — they require an explicit verse.

slides.title: 🎗️ One Karet, Two Prohibitions
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya's general rule
rows: Wherever two separate prohibitions share a single stated karet, an unwitting transgressor of both owes two sin offerings — split the sin offering between them
Two prohibitions in Exodus 30:32 — blending it (מְפַטֵּם) and applying it to skin (סָךְ) — but only one karet in 30:33
The mishna lists blending oil, then blending incense, then applying oil — placing incense between the two oil clauses
Just as blending incense is its own independent karet violation, so blending oil and applying oil, though sharing one verse's karet, are independent — two sin offerings

callout.label: Question raised:
callout.text: If prohibitions can split this way without a separate karet verse for each, why did the Torah bother writing karet for one's sister separately at all (Lev. 20:17)? Answer: for the Rabbis, to teach 'no punishment by inference'; for Rabbi Yitzḥak, to render one liable to three offerings for a woman who is sister, father's sister, and mother's sister at once.

slides.title: 🚻 Who Could Transgress All Thirty-Six?
slides.subtitle: The list mixes cases only a man can do with one only a woman can do

nodes.content: ❓ Rabbi Yoḥanan says the tally teaches liability for each of 36 if done in one lapse — but who could do all 36? A man cannot bring an animal upon himself (a woman's act); a woman cannot lie with a male or an animal (two men's acts)

💡 Rabbi Yoḥanan: the list is really about men. Drop 'a woman who brings an animal upon her' and add instead 'a male who brings another male upon him' — per Rabbi Yishmael's view that this is a second, independent prohibition

columns.label: Rabbi Yishmael
columns.content: Derives active and passive male intercourse from two separate verses (Lev. 18:22 and Deut. 23:18) — two sin offerings possible

columns.label: Rabbi Akiva
columns.content: Derives both from one verse (reading תִּשְׁכַּב as both active and passive) — only one sin offering

nodes.content: ✅ Abaye: bestiality can't be split this way even for Rabbi Yishmael, since 'sodomite' (Deut. 23:18) applies only to men — so only the homosexual case gets the extra clause

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: The mishna's list, properly read, describes prohibitions a single man could violate in one unwitting lapse.

slides.title: 3️⃣3️⃣+3️⃣ Rav's Structure of the Mishna
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav: not all 36 are the same kind of case

steps.content: 1️⃣ The mishna really teaches 33 transgressions for which a man is liable to a sin offering when done unwittingly
2️⃣ Then it adds 3 more just to round out the full count of 36 karet violations: a woman who brings an animal upon her, failing to bring the Paschal offering, and failing to circumcise

3️⃣ Proof: the last two are positive mitzvot — but a baraita teaches that a sin offering for unwitting sin applies only where the transgression is a 'sit and do nothing' violation, like idolatry (from Numbers 15:29–30) — not failure to perform a positive act
4️⃣ So Pesach and circumcision carry karet for willful non-performance, yet no sin offering for unwitting non-performance — they belong to the 'completing the count' group of three, not the 33

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: The mishna's single list actually blends two different kinds of items: 33 true sin-offering cases and 3 karet-only cases added purely to reach the number thirty-six.

slides.title: 🔮 Necromancer In, Sorcerer Out
slides.subtitle: Why does the mishna's karet list mention only the necromancer (בַּעַל אוֹב), not the sorcerer (יִדְּעוֹנִי)?

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan
items: Both are stated together in one prohibition (Lev. 19:31) — 'do not turn to the necromancers and the sorcerers'
One prohibition, one offering — the mishna need only list one of the pair
Necromancer is listed because the verse opens with him

boxes.title: Reish Lakish
items: The sorcerer's act involves no physical action — the bone speaks on its own, so no sin offering applies at all
The necromancer's arm-striking counts as an action (per Rabbi Akiva's minimal-action standard)
Rav Pappa: for stoning the two are listed separately since the death penalty divides differently than the prohibition does

callout.label: Underlying dispute:
callout.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, who needs no action at all for a sin offering (hence blasphemy, mere speech, is also excluded only by its own explicit verse); Reish Lakish holds even Rabbi Akiva requires a minor action, which sorcery lacks entirely.

summary.principle: The mishna's tally of thirty-six is not a simple count: some cases split into separate offerings from a single karet verse, others were added only to complete the number, and every omission or inclusion in the list reflects a precise halakhic reason.

flowSteps.content: 🚫 Punishment is never derived by a fortiori logic — only an explicit verse creates liability
🎗️ Rabbi Elazar: two prohibitions sharing one karet still yield two sin offerings (anointing oil)
🚻 The list must describe a man's transgressions; Rabbi Yoḥanan swaps in male-on-male intercourse per Rabbi Yishmael

columns.content: 3️⃣3️⃣+3️⃣ Rav: 33 true sin-offering cases plus 3 added only to complete the count of 36
🔮 Sorcerer omitted from karet list — shares one prohibition with necromancer, or lacks any action

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: every number and every omission in a mishna's list is halakhically deliberate, never incidental

quiz.q: According to the initial answer in the Gemara, why can't karet for intercourse with a full sister (both father's and mother's daughter) be derived by a fortiori inference from the half-sister cases?
o: Because a full sister is not really forbidden
Because punishment is never administered on the basis of a fortiori inference alone
Because the half-sister cases do not carry karet either
Because Rabbi Yitzḥak forbids all logical inferences
quiz.e: The Gemara's rule is that one does not administer punishment (karet) based on an a fortiori inference — an explicit verse is required, even though Rabbi Yitzḥak himself disagrees with this principle.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Elazar's (in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya) rule about two prohibitions that share a single stated karet?
o: The transgressor is entirely exempt from any offering
One who unwittingly transgresses both owes only one sin offering
One who unwittingly transgresses both owes a separate sin offering for each
The rule applies only to the anointing oil and nowhere else
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar teaches that wherever two distinct prohibitions are covered by one karet verse — like blending and applying the anointing oil — the sin offering is split, yielding two separate offerings.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan resolve the problem that the mishna's 36 cases mix acts only a man could do with an act only a woman could do?
o: He says the mishna is simply inconsistent and unreliable
He removes the case of a woman bringing an animal upon herself and substitutes a male who brings another male upon him, per Rabbi Yishmael
He says women are also included in every one of the 36 cases
He deletes the case of male homosexual intercourse entirely
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan reads the mishna as describing a man's possible transgressions, replacing the female bestiality case with the case of a male passively brought into intercourse by another male, following Rabbi Yishmael's view that this is an independent prohibition.

quiz.q: According to Rav's explanation (via Rabbi Elazar), what are the two categories that together make up the mishna's 36 cases?
o: 18 cases for men and 18 for women
33 cases that carry a sin offering for unwitting violation, plus 3 more added only to complete the count of karet violations
36 identical cases with no distinction
30 cases of forbidden relations plus 6 unrelated cases
quiz.e: Rav's structure: 33 genuine sin-offering cases, plus three more (female bestiality partner, failure to bring the Paschal offering, failure to circumcise) added purely to round out the total of 36 karet violations.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, does the mishna's karet list mention the necromancer but not the sorcerer?
o: Because sorcery is not actually forbidden
Because both are stated together in a single prohibition (Leviticus 19:31), so only one need be listed
Because the sorcerer's punishment is not karet but stoning
Because sorcery was added later and postdates the mishna
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that since the necromancer and sorcerer are both included in one verse's prohibition, listing one covers both; Reish Lakish instead explains the omission as due to sorcery lacking any physical action.
